documents.title: Draft memo to Leonard: ideas for education coverage
documents.subject: Unsigned draft memo (to 'Leonard') pitching stories on education as big business: textbook selling (Paul Samuleson/Samuelson), subliminal/corporate advertising in D.C. schools
documents.notes: Standalone typewritten page marked '17' in pen at top right, with handwritten edits (deletions and insertions). Not related in content to the salary documents around it; appears to be a Post editorial-planning memo, possibly repurposed as an exhibit. Photo shows the sheet on a wooden table.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten top right: 17]

Leonard --

I think our metropolitan area coverage of education is fine as far as it goes, but I don't think it goes far enough.

One whole type of stories we could do more with is ~~education as big business~~ For instance:

-- the selling of a textbook. Textbooks are big business, and getting one adopted by a major school systems means big money. That's what made Paul Samuleson a rich man. Stories we could do ~~include~~ [handwritten insertion: an overview of the economics of the business, ] what the current bestsellers are and the process [struck word] of making them into bestsellers -- promotion including bookfairs and wooing high school english teachers on the selection committees. We might be able to find a local textbook author and write about how a grammar text written over many summers has provided a nest egg for retirement. It would be interesting, too, to find out in how many systems Roots is now text.

-- subliminal advertising in the schools. A D.C. school board member once mentioned the number of freebies that the school system gets from major corporations -- films, pencils, book covers -- I'm not sure what types of items there are. The "Stick-Up-For-Breakfast" stuff that the D.C. schools used included pictures of Tony the Tiger, a Kellogg trademark. I would guess that most corporate-supplied material contains a plug for the corporation's product. There may be nothing wrong with it. The schools may come out winners because of money saved by not having to buy some item. But it would be a good story to know how much of this goes on and in what fashion.

[handproof marks and a downward arrow at foot of page]

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Leibovich was paid slightly less than Mayer on the 1998 salary snapshot, similarly to Mayer on the 1999 salary snapshot, more than Mayer on the 2000 salary snapshot and substantially more than Mayer on the 2001 salary snapshot.

Leibovich was paid less than Skrzycki on the 1998 and 1999 salary snapshots and more than Skrzycki on the 2000 and 2001 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Leibovich came to The Post in the late 1990s as a reporter in Financial News. He became a reporter in Style in 2002. Prior to starting at The Post, Leibovich worked as a reporter for the San Jose Mercury News for a little over three years. He also worked as a reporter for the Boston Phoenix for a little less than five years.
Leibovich is a graduate of the University of Michigan.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Leibovich received approximately a 21 percent increase over his prior salary at the San Jose Mercury News. His starting salary was similar to the salary of Hamilton and Mayer at that time and less than the salary of Skrzycki at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Leibovich received six merit increases -- five of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these five merit increases in the following years: 1998, 1999 and 2000. Leibovich also received approximately a 10% salary increase in 1999 in response to an offer from a competing newspaper.

Explanation:
Leibovich was considered an exceptional writer -- evidenced by his later becoming the political writer for the Style section. He did an outstanding job during his time in Financial News.

Leibovich was a highly marketable reporter who often was approached by other papers and publications. As a result, Leibovich was put on the fast track, which increased his salary. He also received an approximate 10 percent salary increase from The Post in 1999 in response to an offer from a competing newspaper.

documents.title: "Dual pay was incorporated into the contract. And the gap grows wider." — Post Factchers/union salary-disparity handout, p. [-2-]
documents.subject: Advocacy/newsletter-style analysis of salary disparities by race and sex among Washington Post reporters under the 1979 dual-pay contract; cites Donald Graham radio remarks; includes bar chart of median reporter salaries by hire-date cohort
documents.date: approx. mid-1980s (references "today" top minimum $664.35 vs NYT $929.60; hires through 1985 charted)
documents.notes: Typed page footed '-2-', with a vertical label at the right edge reading 'DATA | POST FACTCHECKERS' printed on the underlying sheet. Written in a union/employee-advocate voice ('As a union, we're not'). The first page of this item is NOT in the batch: image 5C74254C is a photo of the table showing only the bottom edge of a page (presumably page -1-) whose visible text matches this article's topic, recorded here as a partial page. Dollar figures transcribed as they appear even where they look odd (e.g. '$954', '$955.58').

pages.transcript:
[Photo mostly of a damaged wooden table surface. At the top edge, the bottom of a typed sheet (on pale blue paper) is visible, angled:]
...more male reporters hired du...
median salary for white female report...
higher than for black male reporters hired...
than for black female reporters.

Dual pay was incorporated in the contract.
And the gap grows wider.

On July 30, 1979, the Post and the union reached agreement on a contract to replace the one that had expired more than three years before. The Post demanded a dual pay system as the price of agreeing to a contract, and dual pay became the rule. The top minimum salary for fully experienced reporters got relatively lower each year, compared with what the minimum was at similar papers such as The New York Times and compared with what reporters who had worked here for several years were earning.

In time the top minimum got so low that the Post was given a free hand in setting salaries. The Post top minimum is $664.35 today compared with $929.60 at The New York Times and compared with the $841.46 minimum that a reporter who was fully experienced and on the payroll here as of March 31, 1976 must be paid.

After dual pay went into effect formally at The Post, the gap in salaries between white male reporters and white female reporters grew greater. The median salary for white males hired during 1980-1984 is $190.16 higher than the median salary for white women reporters hired during the same period. Only five black reporters were hired during that five year period who are still on the payroll.

Management's answer isn't borne out by the facts.

When Donald Graham made a recent radio appearance to defuse criticism that the Post was racist, he was asked about pay disparities here.

"To begin with, reporters at The Washington Post now average slightly over $50,000 a year," he said. "...We're talking about variations among people making pretty good money. Within that, due to some historical circumstances at the Post, on average, not in every case, but on average, the people who have been at the newspaper a longer time make more than people who have been there less."

That's not what the data suggest.

The median salary for white male reporters hired during 1980-1984 ($954) is about the same as the median salary ($955.58) for white female reporters hired more than a decade before during 1965-1969. It is substantially higher than the median salary for black males hired during 1965-1969. The median salary for those veteran black male reporters is $45.11 less than the more recent white male hires.

Longevity and greater experience also don't necessarily count for much for white males. The median salary for white males hired 20 years earlier in 1960 - 1964, is only $39.45 more than the median for white males reporters hired in 1980 - 1984 and $35.81 less than for white males reporters hired in 1975 - 1979.

Another argument that has been made to account for the difference in pay is that the Post is hiring older, more experienced white males.

Based on the birth dates of those reporters hired during 1980-1984, the median age of the white males was 34; the median age of the white women was 33, and the median age of the black reporter was 41 [struck/garbled: "II. It appears"] unlikely that the white males were significantly more experienced than the other hires.

CHART: REPORTERS (legend: WHITE MALES, BLACK MALES, WHITE FEMALES, BLACK FEMALES; y-axis MEDIAN SALARIES from 600 to $1,100; x-axis HIRED in cohorts 55-59, 60-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85; grouped bar chart, values not individually labeled)

Newsroom management has cited "merit and the marketplace" as important determinants of what individuals are paid. The Post seems to be comfortable ratifying the discrimination that prevails in the marketplace. As a union, we're not. We think that women and minorities should be able to walk into the Post and command the same salaries as a white male with comparable experience walking into the Post.

-2-

[vertical text on strip of underlying sheet at right edge:] DATA | POST FACTCHECKERS
